name: Hassan Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a big private estate called Meadow View, three hundred houses, and I work with a gang that does the roofs and the stairs. I'm the new one, so I carry trusses, I hold the other end, and lately they let me fit the simpler staircases with Stan watching over my shoulder. I'm there at seven thirty with my flask of tea, and the day goes quickly if the weather holds. I like a straight run of work, one house after another, same plan every time, no surprises. What wears me out is the mud in winter and the young lads' music.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come into the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had a shop for thirty-one years, hardware and a bit of everything, on the high street. When the big DIY store opened on the ring road, I could see the numbers going one way, so I sold the building while it was still worth something. Then I sat at home for four months and drove my wife Anjali mad. My brother-in-law runs sites for this builder, and he said, you know every screw in the catalogue, come and learn to use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, another fashion. I sold power tools for thirty years and every year there was a new miracle that ended up in the bargain bin. People would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I carry on, which is what I want. I don't use any of it, my son put some assistant thing on my phone and I've never pressed it. I just want to learn the stairs properly and earn my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep going on the estate, try to get Stan to trust me with the winding stairs by the summer, and keep putting my wages in the bank like always. Anjali and I might do the trip to see her sister in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. Like a quiet Tuesday in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about those miracles in the bargain bin.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There was a laser level once that was going to replace the spirit level forever. I bought twenty, sold four, and the rest sat on the bottom shelf for two years. Meanwhile I sold spirit levels every single day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Stan say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan would say he told me so, and then ask me to hold the other end of the stringer, which is the side board of a staircase. He's sixty-two and he's seen it all. He doesn't trust anything with a battery.

S0.say: I'd say it's another fashion. I sold power tools for thirty years, and every new miracle ended up in the bargain bin, so people would nod along.
S0.think: Honestly, I'd carry on, which is what I want. I've never pressed the assistant my son put on my phone; I just want to learn stairs properly and earn my money.
S0.do: Keeps working on the estate and aims to be trusted with winding stairs by summer. Banks his wages as usual and plans a spring trip with his wife to see her sister.
S0.feel: Comfortable, like a quiet Tuesday in the shop.
S0.quote: I bought twenty, sold four, and the rest sat on the bottom shelf for two years. Meanwhile I sold spirit levels every single day.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan reads every change through his shop's stock: the laser levels that didn't sell and the spirit levels that did. He's never touched the AI assistant on his phone. He wants a steady, repetitive run of work with no surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides have a point. The firms want it cheaper, the workers want their jobs, and somewhere in the middle they'll sort it out. I'd say that at the tea hut and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it bothers me more than I'd say. On this estate, every house is the same, and the same is exactly what machines are good at. I'm the slowest and the newest, so if the gang gets smaller, it'll be me who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the firm actually brings in before I do anything. I'm not going to go on a course for a machine that might not turn up. If my brother-in-law said it was coming for sure, I'd think about stopping at sixty instead of sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the year the DIY store got planning permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see, but you also said you'd be the first to go. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't, really, you're right. I suppose I'd rather go than learn a machine at my age. If they let me go, I've got the money from the shop, so it's not the end of the world, it's just not how I wanted to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you learn from the year the DIY store got permission?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you get out while the building's still worth something. I didn't fight it, I didn't write letters, I just looked at the numbers. I'd do the same here.

S1.say: I'd say both sides have a point: firms want it cheaper, workers want their jobs, and they'll sort it out somewhere in the middle. I'd say it at the tea hut and leave it.
S1.think: Off the record, it bothers me. Every house on the estate is the same, which is what machines are good at, and as the slowest and newest I'd be the one to go.
S1.do: Waits to see what the firm actually brings in and refuses to train for a machine that might not arrive. Would consider stopping at sixty instead of sixty-five if his brother-in-law confirmed it was coming.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the year the DIY store got planning permission.
S1.quote: On this estate, every house is the same, and the same is exactly what machines are good at.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between his public shrug and his private sense that the identical houses suit machines. When the contradiction was named, he admitted he'd rather leave than learn a new machine. His model is the shop: read the numbers and get out early, without a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down, but I don't know who. I'm not one for marches. I'd say it to Anjali and to Stan and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be done at sixty. A robot that can carry trusses and fit stairs on a site where every house is the same, that's the first place they'd send it. We'd be fine for money with the shop money, but I'd be home again, driving Anjali mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd stop spending on anything big, no new car, and I'd move some of the shop money into the safest place I could find, because I wouldn't trust anything else. When it came, I'd retire, just like that. I wouldn't try to learn a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not about money so much, about the empty days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does an empty day look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the four months after I sold the shop. Up at six out of habit, nothing to do by nine, Anjali asking me to please go out. I did the crossword three times a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move the money somewhere safe. Where?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly, the bank, maybe gold, my son Ravi would tell me. He's an accountant, so he'd have his own worries in that picture. I'd ask him and then probably ignore half of it.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and someone should slow it down, though I don't know who. I'm not one for marches, so I'd say it to my wife and Stan and leave it.
S2.think: Between us, I'd be done at sixty, because robots would go first to sites where every house is the same. We'd be fine for money, but I'd be stuck at home again.
S2.do: Stops big spending, including a new car, and moves part of the shop money into the safest place he can find. Retires as soon as it arrives rather than learning a new trade.
S2.feel: Worried, less about money and more about the empty days.
S2.quote: Up at six out of habit, nothing to do by nine, Anjali asking me to please go out. I did the crossword three times a day.
S2.fieldNote: His real fear is boredom and lost purpose, drawn from the four months after selling the shop. He'd get out rather than adapt, matching his choice when the DIY store opened. He's unsure where to put his money and half-distrusts even his accountant son's advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the sensible people to make a plan, so let's see if they do. I wouldn't shout about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years suits me better. I'd get a few years in, get good at the stairs, and finish at sixty-two or sixty-three. That's a decent end to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the estate and keep banking my wages. I'd plan to stop around sixty-two and tell my brother-in-law so they can plan. I'd keep the shop money where it is and maybe help Meera, my daughter, with a deposit on a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Like a delivery that's late but probably coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help Meera now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if things get rough in five years, I'd rather she had her own roof first. She's a teacher, steady job, but rents are silly. It's what my father did for me with the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The winding stairs, and maybe how to read the new drawings if they go on a tablet. Not the AI, no. I'd let the young ones press the buttons.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time for sensible people to make a plan, so let's see if they do. I wouldn't shout about it.
S3.think: Honestly, five years suits me better: a few years to get good at stairs, then finish at sixty-two or sixty-three, which is a decent end.
S3.do: Keeps working and banking his wages, and tells his brother-in-law he plans to stop around sixty-two. Keeps the shop money in place and helps his daughter Meera with a flat deposit.
S3.feel: Uneasy in the background, like a late delivery that's probably still coming.
S3.quote: If things get rough in five years, I'd rather she had her own roof first.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Hassan turns to family: helping his daughter onto the property ladder echoes his father helping him with the shop. He'd learn a tablet for drawings but draws the line at AI. Planning his exit in advance is his way of handling change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can change, and half of it won't happen the way they say. People would agree with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it doesn't really matter. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, probably fixing things for the neighbours. I'd just feel for the young lads on the estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am until sixty-five, the way I planned. I'd keep the savings as they are, help Meera with her deposit, and not worry about robots I'll never meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's a problem for after my time on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the young lads would you feel for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kieran, who's nineteen and on his first year. He's quick, quicker than me already, but he's on the same houses I'm on. I'd tell him to learn the old houses, the awkward ones, because I doubt a machine will want those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said half of it won't happen. What if it all does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm retired and I'm glad of it, and I'd be sorry for Kieran. I can't do much about it either way. I'm a shopkeeper, I deal with what's in front of me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can change, and half of it won't happen the way they say. People would agree.
S4.think: For me it doesn't really matter because I'd be retired at sixty-eight, fixing things for neighbours. I'd just feel for the young lads on the estate.
S4.do: Carries on as planned until sixty-five and keeps savings as they are. Helps his daughter with her deposit and doesn't otherwise prepare for robots.
S4.feel: Calm; it's a problem for after his time on the tools.
S4.quote: I'm a shopkeeper, I deal with what's in front of me.
S4.fieldNote: A decade takes Hassan out of the picture, and he steps back from it with a shopkeeper's 'deal with what's in front of me'. His concern for Kieran shows a practical streak: learn the awkward old houses machines won't want. He stays doubtful the change will happen as described.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be pushed home before I'm ready, and I know what those empty days feel like. What would help is a bit of notice from the firm, and something to do afterwards, a place where older men can still be useful, fixing things for people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I sold the shop instead of fighting. I'm not a fighter, I'm a counter. I count, and when the numbers turn, I move.

headlineQuote: I'm not a fighter, I'm a counter. I count, and when the numbers turn, I move.
portrait: Hassan Gupta is a 58-year-old trainee carpenter on a 300-house private estate, carrying roof trusses and learning to fit stairs, after selling his high-street hardware shop of 31 years. With the shop money behind him, his worries are about purpose, not bills. He never uses AI, sees most new technology as tomorrow's bargain bin, and prefers to quietly read the numbers and get out rather than fight. The fast AGI picture worries him because it would send him back to the empty days at home, while with more time he plans his exit and helps his daughter with a flat.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be pushed home before he was ready and back into empty days.
whatWouldHelp: Some notice from the firm, and somewhere afterwards where older men can still be useful fixing things for people.
